Uniform Title: Vijñānabhairava Manuscript: BHU C4245 Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: April 7, 2012. Country of Publication: India.
This *Vijñānabhairavabhaṭṭāraka* is now being written.
Oṃ, homage to the Supreme Bhairava!
"O Lord, I have heard everything originating from the Rudrayāmala, including the divisions of the Trika in its entirety, categorized according to the essence of the essences. (1)
Even now, O Supreme Lord, my doubt has not ceased:
regarding Bhairava, who possesses a terrifying form, does he exist through a ninefold nature? (2)
Is it a self divided by the three heads, or is it composed of the three powers? Is it consisting of *nāda* and *bindu*, or is it the moon that obstructs the earth? (3)
Or whether the mind is mounted upon the wheel, or whether it has the nature of the *śakti*; or again, whether it pertains to the entire *parāparā* or to the *aparā*.
If it were like that [i.e., like the self], then its being "prior" would be contradicted;
for [priority] could not exist through a distinction of letters or a distinction of bodies. (5)
"Otherness arises from being partless or having parts;
O Lord, grant me grace and sever my doubt entirely. (6)
"Excellent, excellent! You have asked well regarding this essence of the tantra, O beloved. It is most strictly to be concealed, O auspicious lady; nevertheless, I shall tell it to you."
Whatever complete form of Bhairava has been proclaimed,
O Goddess, that should be understood as being without essence, like a web of wheels.
It is like an illusion, a dream, and the delusion of a city of Gandharvas;
it is for the sake of meditation for those of deluded intellect who abide in the ostentation of ritual actions.
This has been described merely for the sake of men whose minds are struck down by conceptual construction;
in reality, this Navātman is neither the mass of sounds nor Bhairava.
Nor is the god Triśiras, nor is he composed of the three powers;
he is not divided by the sequence of the wheels, nor is he of the nature of power. || 11 ||
For those of unawakened minds, these are merely terrors for children;
everything has been taught for the sake of engagement, like a mother’s sweetmeat.
Freed from the measurement of space and time, and devoid of specific spatial designations,
it cannot be designated by any power whatsoever in the ultimate sense.
Within, she is the bliss of one's own experience, whose sphere of perception is liberated from conceptual construction;
she is Bhairavī, the fullness of all states, belonging to the very self of Bhairava. (14)
That body should be known in its true nature as stainless and filling the universe;
when the supreme reality is of such a character, who is there to be worshipped, and who can be satiated? (15)
The state of Bhairava that is thus celebrated is proclaimed as the Supreme Goddess (Parādevī), who exists in the form of both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Since the non-difference between power and the possessor of power has always existed, therefore, because she possesses his attributes, the Supreme Power belongs to the Supreme Self. (17)
The burning power of fire is not perceived as distinct from the fire itself; it is merely this initial manifestation occurring at the onset of the existence of cognition. (18)
For one who has entered the state of Śakti through undifferentiated contemplation, he then becomes identical with Śiva; this is what is called "facing inward" (caivīmukha) here.
Just as in the world the divisions of the directions and so forth are not known by means of the rays of a lamp or of the sun, even so, O Dear One, Śiva is [perceived] through devotion. (20)
O God of gods, marked with the trident and adorned with a skull-bowl;
you are empty of direction, place, and time, and devoid of all designations.
That power which takes the form of Bharata is perceived as Bhairava;
by what means is his face attained, and how does he become the Supreme Goddess? (22)
O Bhairava, speak to me according to how I correctly understand it.
For the vital breath (prāṇa) moves upward and the individual soul (jīva) moves downward; one should contemplate the nature of emission (visarga).
The two-fold origination occurs in its proper place, and from sustenance (bharaṇa), stability arises. || 24 ||
Whether internal or external, through the cessation of the pair of dualities, O Bhairavī, the body of Bhairava is thus manifested by Bhairavī. (25)
Power, in the form of the vital breath (*marut*), neither goes out nor enters;
it expands within through a state free of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatā*), thus assuming the form of Bhairava. (26)
Whether it be filled with Kumbhītārī or Citā,
at its end that one named Śānta shines forth, preceded by Śakti.
Visualizing [the light] from its very root as a radiance of rays, consisting of subtle and subtler-than-subtle natures,
at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], Bhairava and the others are stilled.
Rising up in succession, one after another, in the form of lightning for each wheel, until it reaches three fist-lengths above; at that point, there is the Great Arising (mahodaya). || 29 ||
Having properly released the twelve revolving [cycles] differentiated by the twelve syllables, through the state of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, one then becomes Śiva.
One should drink that [nectar] with the mantra until the top of the head is filled;
having made the mind free of conceptual construction, there arises the emergence of the all-pervading one at the very summit of all.
For one meditating on the fivefold emptiness within mandalas that have the forms of mind and the feathers of a peacock, there shall be entry into the heart of the unsurpassed emptiness. (32)
By this very sequence, wherever one may contemplate—
whether in the void, the face, the supreme vessel, or within oneself— the Goddess herself becomes absorbed and bestows boons.
Placing the mind within the skull and remaining with eyes closed,
one gradually perceives the supreme object through the firmness of the mind.
The central channel is situated in the middle, like a lotus fiber;
when that Great Goddess is meditated upon, by her the Lord is made manifest. (35)
When the gaze is restrained by the obstruction of the eyebrows and the closing of the gateway [of the eyes],
and when the *bindu* is seen to dissolve sequentially into its center, there is the supreme state of abiding.

Arising from the agitation within the abode, in the form of a subtle flame-like mark, one meditates on the *bindu* at the end of the crest-lock; at the end of the dissolution within the heart, there is absorption (*laya*). (37)
When the sound of the broken [vessel] is heard in the unstruck resonance of the ear-cavity, one who is proficient in the Sound-Brahman (śabdabrahman) attains the Supreme Brahman. || 38 ||
O Bhairavī, through the utterance beginning with the *praṇava* and the meditation on the void at the end of the protracted vowel (*pluta*),
one attains emptiness by means of the supreme power (*parā śakti*) which is itself the void.
Whichever caste one may contemplate as having a prior limit, that person becomes empty through emptiness; such a person is of the nature of emptiness. (40)
When the sounds of stringed instruments and the like are long and established in a sequence,
one whose mind is focused on nothing else will, at the conclusion, become the embodiment of the supreme ether.
Through the subtle sequence of mantra applied to every single aggregate,
Śiva arises from the utterance of the Void (śūnya), which consists of the half-moon, the bindu, and the end of nāda.
One should simultaneously contemplate both within one's own body in all directions;
for him whose mind is free from conceptual construction, the entire sky-like expanse unfolds.

He who meditates simultaneously on the emptiness of the subsequent [state] and the emptiness of the fundamental [state], becomes non-conceptual through that simultaneous absence of conceptualization. || 44 ||
One should meditate for a mere moment on the region of the body as emptiness;
being free from conceptual construction within that which is free from conceptual construction, she partakes of her own true nature. 45.
O fawn-eyed one, if that substance which pervades the entire body were to be manifested as all-pervading, then that meditation upon it would become firm. (46)
For one who meditates thus, there is no difference whatsoever;
he becomes a partaker of that which is to be meditated upon, with his senses dissolved in the space of the heart and situated within the center of the lotus-casket.
With an undistracted mind, O fortunate one, one shall attain supreme good fortune;
one should lead the mind from every part of one's own body to the *dvādaśānta*. (48)
The firm intellect proceeds toward the firmly established mark of reality;
in whatever manner and wherever one casts the mind at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths], [so it shall proceed]. (49)
Day by day, there occurs a transformation in one whose mental fluctuations have been diminished;
for by means of the fire of Time, his own city is consumed from the city of Time. (50)
One should contemplate it as burnt at the end; then there arises the appearance of peace.
In this very way, having meditated upon the entire imagined world as consumed by fire, [one attains tranquility]. (51)

For a person whose mind is focused on nothing else, the supreme state of manhood shall be attained—whether regarding one's own body or the world, including even the most subtle and subtlest things. (52)

Having meditated upon those principles which cause supreme internal anguish when one contemplates hell, and having meditated upon that which is both abundant and difficult to attain within the twelvefold sphere; 53.
Entering into the heart and meditating with focused discipline, one shall attain sovereignty;
through austerity, one should contemplate everything in the form of the worlds and so forth.
Until the dissolution of the mind is granted through the abandonment of both the subtle and the gross, [one must proceed] at the boundaries of this entire universe on all sides. (55)

Having meditated upon the deity of reality through the process of the temporal stages (*adhvaprakriyā*), O Great Goddess, one of great exaltation should contemplate this entire universe as having become void. (56)
Right there, with the mind dissolved in tranquility and becoming a vessel for that absorption, one should cast one's gaze upon a place devoid of trees, mountains, walls, and the like. (57)
When the mental state has dissolved, the flow of mental modifications becomes exhausted;
having understood both states, one should meditate and take refuge in the middle.

And having simultaneously abandoned both, reality shines forth in the middle; if, when an object is abandoned, the mind is restrained and does not move toward another object, [then reality is revealed]. (59)
Then, through that state of being in the center, the meditation blossoms intensely;
for one should contemplate the entire body, or indeed the whole world, as consisting of that.
Simultaneously, through the non-conceptual mind,
there is the supreme arising from the friction of the two winds, whether internally or ultimately externally.
The yogi, possessing the vessel for the emergence of the knowledge of reality, should contemplate the entire world or his own body as filled with his own bliss. (62)
Simultaneously, by means of one's own [innate] delight alone,
through the practice of the hollow (kuhara), one becomes composed of supreme bliss instantly, at the very moment of the deer.
By means of the ocean, the great bliss, that reality is revealed through the binding of all currents and the teachings on the paths of the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*).
At the moment of the ant's touch, there is supreme bliss;
one should cast the mind, filled with bliss, into the midst of the fire's object.
Or it is filled solely with breath and joined with the bliss of Smara;
agitated by union with Śakti, it culminates in the entry of Śakti.

That bliss which belongs to the reality of Brahman is called the bliss of one's own identity; it arises from the memory of the face of a woman, even when she is merely licked, smeared, or touched. (67)
O Goddess of the Gods, even through the mere capacity [to imagine it], there occurs a flood of bliss;
when great bliss is attained, as when a long-lost kinsman is finally seen. (68)

Having meditated upon the bliss that has arisen, one should become absorbed in it and focused on that mind, through the expansion of the bliss of rasa resulting from the effulgence of the burnt-away pride and passion. (69)
From that, the state of being filled arises, and from that, great bliss (mahānanda) occurs;
through the tasting of objects such as song and so forth, the mind becomes solely absorbed in equal happiness.
Because the mind is established in the form of that [object] through identification with it,
wherever the mind creates a mental projection, one should fix the mind right there.
In each such state, the supreme bliss of one's own true nature shines forth,
when sleep has not yet arrived and the external field of perception has vanished.
That state, accessible through the mind, shines as the Supreme Goddess when the power of Īśvara is manifested in the sky by means of the light of the sun, lamps, and so forth. (73)
Having fixed one's vision right there, one's own essential nature shines forth through Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, and Lelihānā. (74)
And at the time of the gaze of Khecarī, the supreme pervasion (parāvyāpti) shines forth;
with the buttock resting on a soft seat, the hands and feet are without support. (75)
By practicing that repeatedly, the mind becomes completely filled with the Supreme.
Sitting properly upon a seat, one should keep the arms slightly bent.
Placing the mind in the space between the armpits, one should contemplate the *samāna* [vāyu];
one should cast the gaze toward the left side of the gross form of the object.
Having made the mind supportless in a short time, one shall go to Śiva;
whether sitting or lying down on a seat, one should contemplate it as being without support.
When the mind has become attenuated, one should cause one's own body to become increasingly attenuated;
or else, while seated on a movable seat, by gradually moving the body. (79)
When the human state has become tranquil, one should attain the divine flood. One should contemplate the entire void, dissolved at the crown of the head, as Bhairava.
All that should enter into the reality-principle (tattva) of the form of Bhairava;
having known even a little of this, there arises again the darkness of the external world.
The wise one, having known the form of Bhairava to be like infinite light,
likewise [perceives] this difficult illusion for a long time at the onset of the dark fortnight.
One should meditate on the form of the cataract; one should meditate so that one becomes Bhairava.
This applies to whichever sense organ there may be, through its obstruction and suppression. (83)
For one who has entered into the non-dual void, that divine Self reveals itself;
he is great as he recites the syllable *A*, which consists of the ocean, the moon, the visarga, and the letter *A*.
O Goddess, the Supreme Lord arises suddenly as a flood of ignorance;
place that [ignorance] within consciousness at the end of the emission of the letter *visarga*. 85.
With a mind free of support, one should touch the eternal Brahman—oneself as the very form of space, unenveloped by the directions—in meditative concentration. (86)
Then, when the consciousness free from latent desires reveals its own nature as power, one should first visualize some part [of the body] with a sharp needle or similar instrument. (87)
In that very state, volition is joined with Bhairava, the stainless path; since there is no beginning or end to the mind and so forth, one should contemplate it as being entirely within. || 88 ||
By the absence of conceptual names, one becomes abandoned by conceptual constructions;
by me, the "delusive" power of the creative impulse (kalā) has been established.
Having observed that a desire for worldly existence has arisen, one should bring it to rest.
From whatever source it has arisen, into that very source it dissolves;
when it arises from the desire for the Unripe (āmam), then I am indeed Speech (vāk) as Knowledge (jñāna).
In reality, at that time, I have become that; my mind becomes absorbed in that.
Or, when desire or knowledge has arisen, one should settle the consciousness [therein]. (92)
When the mind is not occupied with anything else due to the notion of a self, then the vision of the reality of the self becomes a supportless knowledge,
free from causal conditions and devoid of the nature of delusion.
O beloved, according to the reasoning of reality, Śiva is consciousness itself, all-pervading;
as the attribute of consciousness within all bodies, there is no distinction anywhere.
Therefore, a person desiring liberation should contemplate everything as being composed of that [Brahman], even while within the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (95)
Having rendered the intellect free from agitation, that very reality remains;
the universe, consisting of a magical illusion, is laid down like a painted picture.
Whether wandering, meditating, or seeing everything, there is the arising of happiness;
one should not cast the mind into suffering, nor should one be carried away by pleasure. 97.
O Bhairavī, when [all] has been withdrawn into the center, what reality remains? One should contemplate, "I am not," having abandoned everything residing within one's own body. (98)
With a firm mind and a vision that does not look for anything else, one should become happy;
for the cognition regarding a jar or similar objects, as well as desire and so forth, exists within the left [channel]. (99)
By meditating on the fact that nothing whatsoever has arisen as omnipresent, one becomes all-pervading;
for the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings. (100)
But for yogins, there is a distinction: they possess attentiveness toward the relationship.
One should cultivate the realization that consciousness exists even in a body other than one's own;
having abandoned even the regard for one's own body, one becomes happy like a woodcutter.
Having made the mind supportless, one should not conceptualize any conceptualization;
O deer-eyed one, that is the state of the Self and the Supreme Self, which is Bhairava.
The omniscient, the creator of all, the pervasive Supreme Lord—he alone is I and the very nature of reality; through such firm conviction, one becomes Śiva. (4)
These various manifestations of the universe are not distinct from me, Bhairava; they are like the waves of water, the flickering flames of fire, or a mass of radiance. || 5 ||
Having wandered and wandered repeatedly within the body, through its swift falling away and the cessation of the power of agitation, the state of Parā arises.
Alternatively, through the support, or by means of power, or through meditation by the surface of the mind,
those who have attained the immersion of power are agitated into the Bhairava body.
O blessed one, O fair-faced lady, listen properly to this tradition:
liberation arises immediately when the eyes are merely fixed in a steady gaze. (8)
By standing in the great abyss that exceeds ten [fathoms] and gazing upward,
O you of non-conceptual mind, the way of the immediate mind becomes perfectly clear.
Wherever the mind goes—whether externally, internally, or in between—in that very place the state of Śiva prevails, because it is all-pervasive. (10)
Wherever the consciousness of the All-pervading Lord is manifested through the path of the senses,
because that [consciousness] has those [senses] as its sole substrate, there arises the state of being the plenum through absorption into Cit.
In hunger and other such states, in fear and sorrow, in a deep abyss, in the flight of an elephant, in leaping, plowing,
and at the end of hunger and so forth— the reality of Brahman is present within the fetter.
When objects are being recollected, one should withdraw the mind from the perceived location;
then the Lord [of the mind], being without support, spreads forth through one's own body.
In some cases, one should gradually withdraw the gaze from an object;
when that knowledge is joined with [the practice], one becomes an abode of emptiness. 14.
The kind of delight experienced by one who is detached due to the abundance of devotion—that is the power of Śaṅkara; therefore, meditate on it constantly, for through that one becomes Śiva. || 15 ||
When another object is being experienced, emptiness gradually [arises] regarding all things.
Having meditated upon that very [emptiness] in this manner, even what was known becomes stilled. (16)
That purity which is taught by those of limited knowledge is not true purity in the vision of Śambhu;
for there is neither pure nor impure. Therefore, one should be free from conceptual construction and happy.
In all things, the state of Bhairava exists within the common range of perception; and since there is no other reality apart from that, this is the realization of non-duality. 18.
One should be equal toward enemy and friend, and equal in honor and dishonor;
knowing this to be due to the perfect fullness of Brahman, one should be happy. (19)
One should not cultivate hatred, nor should one ever cultivate passion. Freed from both passion and hatred, one moves toward Brahman in the state of the middle way.
Whatever is to be known, whatever is to be grasped, whatever is empty, and whatever is understood—all that should be contemplated as Bhairava; at its end, it arises as the Obstruction (rodha).
Having fixed the mind upon the external space— which is eternal, desireless, empty, all-pervading, and devoid of mental construction— one should enter the spaceless state.
Wherever the mind goes, that very thing is not its true characteristic;
by abandoning it and abiding in the new state, one then becomes free from waves.
"Because he causes everything to act and makes everything resound throughout the entire universe, Śiva is [known] by the continuous utterance of the word Bhairava. (24)
"I am that very person," and so forth, arises from the context of practice;
for the mental continuum, being without a physical basis, is calmed through the impelling force of that meditation. (25)
Eternal, all-pervading, without support, and the sovereign lord of all—he meditated at every moment on words according to their intended meaning. (26)
All this that exists is unreal, appearing like a magician’s trick;
what is the reality behind a magician’s trick? Thus one should proceed with firm conviction. (27)
Where is there knowledge or action for the self, which is changeless?
Since external objects are extended through knowledge, this world is therefore empty.
"Neither my bondage nor my liberation exists; these are merely terrors of that very [mind].
This is a reflection of the intellect, like that of the sun in waters. (29)
All contact with pleasure, pain, and so forth is mediated by the senses;
thus, having abandoned the senses, one remains established in oneself, abiding in the Self. (30)
All knowledge is illuminating, yet the Self is the illuminator of all;
because its very nature is such, it is conceived as both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
When the quartet consisting of the mind, volition, power,
and the self has completely perished, that is the body of Bhairava.
O Goddess, there are one hundred and twelve waveless instructions in brief; having known these, the wise man becomes a knower of wisdom.
And when this very heat is joined [with practice], Bhairava himself is born;
through speech he performs actions, bestowing both curses and favors. (34)
Endowed with qualities such as youthfulness and the rest, he attains freedom from old age and death;
O Goddess, he is beloved by the Yoginīs and is the sovereign lord of all melāpas.
Even while living, he is liberated, even while performing his activities.
"O God, O Maheśvara, if this body belongs to another, who is it that performs the recitation when there is no such established state, and what is that recitation? (37)
This is the method here that I shall describe for you, O fawn-eyed one, regarding the gross [levels] alone,
as to how contemplation is repeatedly cultivated toward the supreme reality.
In meditation, that intellect which is immovable, formless, and without support is [true meditation];
meditation is not the body and so forth, nor the conceptualization of faces, hands, and so on. (39)
Whatever firm devotion is cultivated by people through offerings such as food and flowers, that indeed is worship of the supreme, non-conceptual void; for it is absorption therein. (40)

In the fire of dissolution, which is the Great Void, the elements, the senses, the objects, and so forth, are offered together with the mind; that is the oblation, with consciousness as the sacrificial ladle. (41)
O Supreme Goddess, in this sacrifice, satisfaction is characterized by bliss;
it is so called, O Pārvatī, because of the destruction of all sins and the protection of all.
The immersion into the power of Rudra is that supreme field of contemplation;
otherwise, what worship could there be for that inert [object], and who would be satisfied? (43)
Whatever substances are used for worship or for satisfying the Supreme and the Non-Supreme, and whoever is the worshipper—all that is indeed the single act of worship. (44)
The vital breath (prāṇa) may depart and the individual soul (jīva) may enter; the crooked action arises from desire.
She is the long-souled Great Goddess, the supreme and yet non-supreme, who enters the field of another. 45.
Following this, one should remain in the sacrifice consisting of great bliss;
thus possessed by the deity, one shall attain the supreme Bhairava. || 46 ||
Six thousand and twenty-one thousand recitations of the Goddess are prescribed for day and night; this is extremely difficult to achieve at the end of one's life. (47)
Thus, O Goddess, has this supreme and most excellent nectar been declared;
and this must never be revealed to anyone at any time.
In all other cases—where one is cruel, lacks devotion at the feet of the Guru, or is among those of fixed intellect who are "heroes" (vīras) with haughty minds—[this applies]. (49)
To the devotees and the assembly of gurus, one should give without hesitation a village, a kingdom, another country, or sons, wives, and family. 50.
O fair-eyed one, having renounced all this, you must grasp this;
even your life-breaths should be given away, but the supreme nectar must not be given.
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Śaṅkara, I am completely satisfied; the Rudrayāmala mantra has been fully mastered by me today.
Furthermore, the heart of all the various divisions of power has been understood this very day.
Having spoken thus, the goddess, filled with joy, threw her arms around Śiva’s neck.
